keyFindings.description: Security[secret]: the retag-again remedy, which is new this round and not something round 3 asked for, licenses storing credential material on a condition that is silently false on Secret Manager. The bullet says 'The remedy is to run the retag again and require another exit 0 with none of those lines after it', and the paragraph's eventual-consistency caveat is stated only of the answering process, where staleness surfaces as exit 1 because rereadRetag compares the kind it reads back (cmd/agent-secrets/secret_retag.go:178-187). A peer's staleness surfaces as nothing. The peer's notification-driven reread is a direct read too (reread/reread.go:173-176 calls RefreshOne, which reads the one name), and on Secret Manager a direct read is eventually consistent (secrets/gcp.go:185-188), so a peer can receive the notification, read successfully, still hold the ordinary-secret policy, and log nothing: reread.go:175 warns only when Refresh returns an error, and a successful read of the old tags is not an error. The notification is also asynchronous, so even a healthy peer has not necessarily applied the retag when the answering pod returns 200 (handlers_secrets.go:126-135 sends the NOTIFY and returns its own Lookup). So the gate 'another exit 0, no lines' can be met while a peer still releases the stored value raw to a grant made before the conversion, which is the case the whole paragraph exists to prevent. Two sentences close it, and no fence or code is needed: say that a peer's reread can succeed and still read the old tags, silently, so no line and no exit 0 establishes the peers; and give the sound alternative, which is to create the secret with its kind from the start rather than converting a name agents already hold grants on. This is a judgement about residual risk on a documented procedure rather than a defect in code: if the architect judges the residual acceptable and wants the paragraph as it stands, I will record that ruling and approve.

'A reread is the whole broker's, not one process's' covers both mechanisms the paragraph before it names, and only one of them fans out. The automatic miss-path reread calls Policy.RefreshOne and updates that process alone (requests/machine_state.go:371-378); the notification is attached to the HTTP handler and nowhere else (api/handlers_secrets.go:126-129), which handlers_secrets.go:121-125 states deliberately. Scope the sentence to POST /v1/secrets/{name}/reread and say the miss path stays local.

The redial row says a pod logging it 'goes on answering /healthz 200 and serving the whole time'. /healthz pings Postgres and answers 503 DATABASE_UNAVAILABLE when that fails (api/server.go:361-363), and the most common cause of a lost LISTEN connection is the database being unreachable, so the two can appear together. The point the row is making is right and worth keeping: losing the LISTEN does not by itself fail readiness. Say that rather than promising 200.

'A payload this build cannot read, and a name the reread refuses, are each dropped with one WARN and nothing else' is right for the first and wrong for the second. A policy refusal is not an error: Loader.LoadOne logs its own RefusedMessage and returns a Lookup carrying the reason with a nil error (policy/load.go:171-173), RefreshOne merges it and returns nil (policy/current.go:144-156), and main's callback discards the Lookup and returns only the error (cmd/broker/main.go:317-319), so :175's WARN never fires for a refused name. What this package drops with one WARN is an unreadable payload and a failed Refresh call.

Three statements about the stop path claim more than the code gives. ':532-536' says the listener 'is ended before the store is closed' and that closing the store 'releases that connection': endServing() only requests cancellation and nothing waits for the listener goroutine, and the connection is hijacked out of the pool (store/store.go:121-125), so st.Close() never touches it — pglisten's own deferred close does (pglisten/listener.go:146,218-221). This is the comment I raised in round 1 as a Fast-follow item and it is still standing. ':239' and ':530-531', and operate.md:416-417, say the loops run until 'the last request has been answered'; srv.Shutdown returns its context's error when the 60-second allowance expires first (main.go:527-538 logs it and proceeds), so the loops run until Shutdown completes or that allowance runs out. And ':592-600', with operate.md:363,387-390 and AGENTS.md:3034-3037, calls writeTimeout 'the longest exchange the server itself allows' covering 'every request the server ever let in': Go resets the write deadline after the request headers are read, and this server allows ten seconds for headers separately (main.go:482), so 60 seconds bounds the post-header exchange rather than the whole accepted connection.

piLegionRed: pi-legion is completed failure at the code head (job 121144366399), on packages/pi-legion/src/skills-guard.test.ts:36, naming skills/legion-architect/SKILL.md at 51256 bytes over Oh My Pi's spill threshold. It is not this change's: the pull request touches no file under skills/ (gh pr diff --name-only | grep -c skills/ is 0), the same lane was success at the two previous code heads, and the guard passes in this workspace at this head (bun test packages/pi-legion/src/skills-guard.test.ts: 10 pass, 0 fail). GitHub runs pull_request workflows on the merge of head into base, and that file is 51256 bytes on main against 50986 on this branch — exactly the figure CI reported. So main grew the skill past the guard, every pull request's merge tree now trips it, and merging this one does not fix it. It is not a required check, so it blocks neither the daemon nor READY. Raised to the architect with this evidence; a problem outside this issue is a dispatch ask and never an issue I file.

What remains is the retag-again bullet added beside them, which is this round's finding.
Finding 2: operate.md:365 no longer calls the redial warning the only signal; it names the three other rows and which two can be matched to a secret.
Finding 3: main.go:243-245 now says the pod returns without draining at all, and :265-266 now says what is saved is the drain rather than a minute nobody pays.

Finding 4: secondSignalFindsServing's comment and the ERROR line both say the broker had not begun serving when the second signal was read, and the comment states plainly that a lock or a second check there would be a fix to a window that does not need one — which is what the architect ruled.
Finding 5: the oauth row's comment now describes two callers over one pool rather than two pods, and credits storetest.Open's ping with the warmed connection.

thermonuclear.deepReview: CHANGES — one High, the retag-again remedy, reached independently and marked as not sourced from the discussion; it is this round's finding 1. No other finding: go build and go vet clean, and no defect in the reread route's buckets, the drain, the watchdog, the catch-up, the NOTIFY path, the hijacked connection or the CI job.
thermonuclear.codeQuality: CHANGES — the comment-against-code sweep is not clean for the fourth round running: concepts.md's fleet-wide claim covering the miss path, operate.md's /healthz 200 promise, reread.go's refused-name claim, and the three stop-path statements, all taken as findings 2 to 5. Structural items — main.go at about 650 lines with the boot and stop sequence inline, limits.go at 316 mostly comment — stay in the one Fast-follow.

fastFollow: One cleanup item, carried forward: make pglisten.Owner required and drop owner()'s fallback; share the hijacked one-connection listener pool between internal/broker/store and internal/dispatch/store/pool.go; fold brokertest.Rig onto the new Client; default NotifyReread and Draining in api.Register; move the boot and stop sequence into cmd/broker/shutdown.go; move the OAuth provider-secret read above the bind; keep one canonical copy of the reread sizing derivation; and state the fan-out's guarantee the same way in all five places that state it. The cleanup that would end the class these rounds keep finding is the decomposition itself: four sweeps have each found more prose drift in a change whose comments outweigh its code, and less prose beside smaller functions is the remedy that scales where another sweep does not.
